sections.content:
Course Description:
The overall objective of this course is to provide students with a practical introduction of the
fundamental knowledge and theories of human resources management (HRM), ranging from
strategic planning, acquiring, evaluating, training, to rewarding human resources.
The course contributes to the following learning goals for the BBA in MGMT:
1. Graduates will be critical and creative thinkers who make effective decisions supported by
analytical techniques.
2. Graduates will be effective communicators in oral and written English for general business
applications.
3. Graduates will have broad understanding of the core business functions and integrate these
functions to solve business problems.
4. Graduates will have in-depth grasp of their area of business concentration or major.
5. Graduates will be effective team members and leaders.
6. Graduates will be effective in multi-cultural and international settings.
7. Goal: Graduates will understand their professional and ethical responsibility.

sections.content:
This course provided a solid introduction to basic HR concepts without overwhelming students with complexity. The content was straightforward and easy to grasp, focusing on foundational topics across approximately 13–14 chapters in total. Nothing felt overly advanced or technical, making it accessible even for those new to the subject.
Overall, the course struck a good balance between coverage and depth, prioritizing clear understanding of core HR principles over excessive difficulty. It’s an excellent option for anyone seeking a gentle yet informative entry into human resources topics.
sections.teaching: Tina's teaching style was a highlight of the course. She was friendly and funny, which made her classes engaging and enjoyable rather than dry or monotonous. Her approachable personality helped create a positive classroom atmosphere, and she built strong connections with several students, fostering a sense of community and making it easier for us to participate and ask questions.
sections.grading:
Grading in the course was fair and encouraging, with Tina promising to aim for the best possible outcomes for students' grades. This approach made it straightforward to achieve a decent grade without excessive pressure. The assessment breakdown was as follows:

Mid-Term (Multiple Choice Questions and Short Questions) 25%
In-class Participation and Attendance 25%

Group Project Presentation with Individual Performance Assessment and Peer Evaluation 28%

Group Reports (PowerPoint Slides + 1-page Executive Summary)10%

Individual Reflection Report12%
sections.workload: The workload was notably light and manageable throughout the semester. There were no regular assignments or quizzes piling up— the main components were participation, an easy midterm, a single group project, and a simple individual reflection report that was essentially just reflecting on what you learned in the course.

sections.teaching:
Hummm...It's really hard to judge his teaching style! He likes to show off himself and share his stories and personal experiences. He always invites groups to share in every class for participation. His schedule varies -- he may finish one lecture's slides in just one session, but it may take two sessions for another set of slides. His contents slides might only give you half of the understanding, and you certainly need to read the textbook (also what he tells us to do at the beginning of every class).

I guess most people might give him a C, but to me, his stories are quite inspiring and valuable, so I give him a B.
sections.grading:
The TA only released the grade for the midterm exam (MC). And he released it in mid-April (although we took the exam in late March). So no data for the overall grading. As a reference, I've got 16/25 (mean 16.7). No data for the final exam (essay). Work hard as this is the largest part. (61.4% in total)

19.6% is Individual and team presentation. The end-of-term team presentation is only graded as a “pass” or “fail”. And I guess unless you choose to free-ride or you are really off-topic too much, otherwise you can pass. For individual participation, every group is racing to raise their hands to share in class. Just submit your PPT to Canvas if you don't have a chance to present, you can still get those marks.

19.0% is Individual and HRM Practice-based Group reports. The individual class practice questions pack is just an easy point. Remember to take a screenshot at the end of the lectures do all the questions and submit it at the end of the semester. And for the two group projects, I don’t think there’s much difference in the scores of different groups. As a tip, he likes stories. So you might start or elaborate your projects by creating a story if you want to get a higher appraisal

The syllabus does not state that the attendance is graded. But he asks you to fill in the attendance sheet in every class.

The grading is good for me. I got a B+.
sections.workload: Congrats! You don't need to worry about you have nothing to do in this class. "At the end of each class lecture, class practice questions are provided for students to review and to reflect upon the knowledge acquired during studies" (from syllabus), with a minimum of 4 questions and a maximum of 7-8 questions. Also, you have to prepare a PPT for every class sharing, and it can cost you a vast amount of time to discover examples and read cases. Also, you've got three group projects to do. For the first two group projects, they are all in video format, with 1) good vs bad interviews and 2) suggestions for a foreign company to start their business in HK using the concepts you have learned in the class. You can imagine how much time you need to spend to make those videos. Luckily, I've got very good teammates so things become more efficient. Not many guidelines for the team presentation so you might need to take time with your team for the flow and procedures. The workload is definitely the worst thing in this course.  Viva la Vida!

However, since it is a 3-hour class, sometimes we all got bored easily due to his talking speed and no break in between (although he ends classes earlier as a compensation). His PowerPoint has those sound effects which are quite embarrassing but somehow funny.

But at the same time, it makes it harder to differentiate our performance. The 2 exams are the major grade differentiator as the rest of the grading components are too easy to get full score. Overall, not too heavy in terms of workload.

sections.content: Only writing this because I don't think some of the reviews (for 2017-2018 fall sem) are fair. Yes, the professor is boring and the lecture content is pretty much useless (not like I was expecting anything else, I was only taking it just in case I cannot graduate because it was a core course and I knew in Spring sem 2017 the MGMT department suddenly cancelled the other core course), but it is pretty good grade IMO (as long as you ain't dumb).
sections.teaching:
Yeah professor is boring but that's why you can exploit this and get good grade. Bunch of half-wits don't listen in class so if you pay a bit of attention on important parts (stories and fill in the blanks as mentioned in my 'Grading' part), you should be able to get at least an A-range.

And just to be fair to the professor, he is boring but by no means is he a prick. I have seen professors worse than him. He is by far the most lenient and chill professor I have seen. it's just that the students are as good as dead and won't be willing to answer any questions, so don't just blame it on the professor (although I wasn't the ones who answer question either, but hey I got a decent grade out of it)
sections.grading:
There are plenty of course components, but then most of them can be satisfied by simply submitting your assignments and attending classes.

As you can see in the attached syllabus, around 26.45% of the total grade can be achieved by handing in assignments (doubt he reads it I spent like 30 minutes bs-ing) and attending classes (PRS). There are bunch of idiots who managed to submit the work late and lose some points here and there (or miss the PRS... whatever).

There is this presentation that may or may not matter, I was in the first batch of groups to present, which means I had less than one week to prepare the presentation. We hea did our presentation (honestly, less than 1 hour of work from everyone) and it was still better than most people (got like 0.2 marks off highest?).

Main differentiator is the mid term and final. Both are just MC and short essay questions, non-cumulative. MCs are only tricky because sometimes he will ask a question on some 'stories' he tells in class, so whenever he said he has a story, just listen up and jot down the details (won't be in the slides). Also try to look at where he left blanks in the slides and fill it in when he goes through it in class. Otherwise, don't bother listening, not like HRM is complicated anyways, everything is common sense in MGMT. Short questions ain't too bad, in the final he simply used the same question as one of the ones he put in the lecture slides, so I guess just make sure you look at them also.

I got 45/50 (3 marks off high i guess? Mean was like 40, SD like 4.5+?) in mid term, dunno about final but final grade A+. So for the reviews that blame it on bad grading even though you guys got 1SD above mean in mid term, you can suck it, you obviously f**ked it in the final.
sections.workload:
Easy. Even if you have to hard carry the presentation I don't think it's that bad (leave yourself around 3 days to do the presentation is enough --> Our PowerPoints are filled with bullet points.

For mid term and final, just revise a bit beforehand. Pretty good to brush grade from my point of view (obviously you might read other reviews and think otherwise).

sections.grading: The grading is quite good. Maybe around 26-27% A range. As long as you attend lectures and do revision before quizzes, you should get a decent grade.

sections.content: All about HR practices. He mentioned introductory issues concerning laws and ethics and strategic HRM. Then, he talked in detail about recruitment and selection, performance appraisal and training, and compensation. Finally, he also spoke of global HRM. Interestingly, he loved using his 4 cases as examples and applying them in different topics.
sections.teaching: The professor is nice and easy-going. He is willing to listen to students' opinions and change the course requirements accordingly. Some complained that they didn't have enough time in the mid-term exam so he extended the time limit in the final exam by 15 minutes. He usually answered questions quite efficiently and in detail. However, you may find the course boring if you're not interested in the topics because of his voice. He sometimes tended to read directly from the ppt.
sections.grading: I do think his grading policy is good. I got full marks in all the reports and my scores in both quizzes were 1 SD above the mean. I got A-range finally. (He did't say much about our performance in participation)
sections.workload: There were a total of 4 cases, one of which was a team-based project presentation, and the remaining were to be read individually. You had to write a 3-page report for each of them. Although he said he would either give you a full mark or zero mark, most of the students could get full marks. Some people might have their reports deducted few marks though. Basically you just have to attend all lectures because he counted participation heavily by PRS and in-class group exercises. There were at least 2 - 3 PRS questions almost every class. But on balance I would say it is not difficult to handle.
